html:
The Toltecs ruled a state centred on the city of Tula, in the modern Mexican state of Hidalgo, which was at its height from about 950 to 1150.

Tula grew after the decline of Teotihuacan and became the leading city of central Mexico. Its best known monuments are the giant stone warriors, the Atlantes, that once held up the roof of a temple on a pyramid. Its art is full of warriors, eagles and jaguars, and a reclining figure called a chacmool. The city was burned and largely abandoned in the 1100s.

Much of what is told about the Toltecs comes from the Aztecs, centuries later. To them, the Toltecs were the model of civilisation, and the Nahuatl word for Toltec came to mean "artisan". Aztec stories tell of the priest-king Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl, who was driven out of Tula and went east. Aztec rulers claimed Toltec descent to make their rule look ancient and right. Scholars still argue how much of this is history and how much legend.

A real puzzle is the strong likeness between Tula and the Maya city of Chichén Itzá in Yucatán, which has similar warrior columns and chacmools. Whether this came from conquest, trade or a shared fashion is not settled. Either way, it shows how ideas moved across Mesoamerica in the centuries between Teotihuacan and the Aztecs.
sum: The Toltecs ruled a state centred on the city of Tula, in the modern Mexican state of Hidalgo, which was at its height from about 950 to 1150.
